extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers (especially beginning to intermediate writers) learning to choose and manage narrative point of view
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for selecting, establishing, and managing first-, second-, and third-person points of view in fiction, including best practices, common mistakes (e.g., head-hopping, unexpected POV shifts), and when to use each type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish the point of view early
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish the point of view within the first two paragraphs of your story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doing so sets reader expectations and builds trust. If you fail to establish POV early, readers can be jarred and your story's architecture can feel fractured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be consistent; avoid changing POV mid-story
rubrics_metrics.description: Once you pick a point of view, you're stuck with it — do not begin in one POV and then switch to another unexpectedly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not begin with a first-person narrator and then switch to third-person, or abruptly change third-person limited to omniscient. Unexpected POV changes create a jarring experience and threaten reader trust. Exception: deliberate, consistently-handled multi-POV (e.g., long works that maintain a consistent dual-POV structure) can work but are difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filter everything through the chosen POV
rubrics_metrics.description: Point of view filters everything in your story; everything must come from a POV.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If story elements are presented outside the chosen POV, the story is damaged. Keep internal thoughts, observations, and descriptions consistent with the narrative vantage point to preserve suspension of disbelief.

rubrics_metrics.name: First person: limited, biased, intimate perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: First person narration uses I/me/my and is narrated from a character inside the story; it is biased and limited but can deliver high intimacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use first person to create closeness and a distinctive voice. Recognize limitations: the narrator cannot know everything and will present a subjective, possibly unreliable account. Consider unreliable narration as a deliberate device to surprise readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-person narrator must be interesting (likability ≠ requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Your first-person protagonist doesn't have to be morally good, but they must be interesting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers will not stay with a 300-page book listening to a character they don't enjoy. Anti-heroes and flawed narrators work well if their perspective is compelling (example: Holden Caulfield).

rubrics_metrics.name: First person: show, don't tell (avoid over-narration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid spending too much time inside the narrator's head explaining feelings; emphasize what the character does rather than only what they think.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You're allowed to mention mood, but reader trust and attention rely on actions and scenes. Over-explaining internal thought can weaken dramatic tension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second person: use sparingly as an immersive/experimental device
rubrics_metrics.description: Second person (you/your) makes the reader the protagonist and pulls the reader into the action; it's uncommon in fiction but useful for certain effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Second person is effective for immediacy, personalization, and surprise; it's also common in nonfiction, lyrics, and interactive fiction (Choose Your Own Adventure). Try it to stretch your skills, but be aware it's an unconventional choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breaking the fourth wall / brief second-person use
rubrics_metrics.description: Addressing the audience directly (breaking the fourth wall) or using short bursts of second person inside another POV can be an effective device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in drama and some novels show this can be fun and effective; use it deliberately and sparingly so it doesn't undermine the main POV.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third person limited: focus on one viewpoint character at a time
rubrics_metrics.description: Third person limited uses he/she/they but typically stays close to a single character's internal experience in a scene or chapter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the most common commercial-fiction POV. You can have multiple viewpoint characters across a book, but keep the narrative limited to one character's inner life at a time to avoid confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third person omniscient: avoid over-sharing all characters' thoughts
rubrics_metrics.description: Third person omniscient gives access to many or all characters' thoughts, but full omniscience is rare and can be problematic if overused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parsing multiple characters' emotions back and forth can give readers whiplash and destroy dramatic tension. Many authors effectively show thoughts of only one character per scene/chapter even in an omniscient framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid head hopping
rubrics_metrics.description: Head hopping is switching rapidly between different characters' thoughts and perspectives within a scene or paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This jarring technique breaks intimacy with the scene's main character and confuses readers. Try to stay in one character's head per scene, or mark POV shifts clearly with section/chapter breaks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use clear breaks when changing viewpoint characters
rubrics_metrics.description: If you use multiple viewpoint characters, change viewpoints at chapter breaks or section breaks (or another clear structural cue).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most authors change viewpoint each chapter; some change on section breaks. Always provide a break to prepare the reader for the shift and prevent accidental head-hopping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide and control your level of omniscience
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberately choose how deeply and frequently you will access characters' thoughts and emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether you'll read thoughts frequently and deeply or rarely; be consistent. Excessive omniscience can remove mystery and reduce drama; controlled depth preserves tension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beginner recommendation: prefer first person or third person limited
rubrics_metrics.description: For writers just getting started, first person or third person limited are easier to understand and manage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These POVs reduce complexity and the risk of head-hopping or unintentional omniscience. Experiment with other POVs once comfortable.

rubrics_metrics.name: POV choice determines narrative distance; no single 'best' POV
rubrics_metrics.description: Different POVs create different distances between reader and story; these distances are ranges, not precise rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A third-person narrator can sometimes feel closer than a first-person narrator depending on execution. Choose the POV that matches the effect you want — intimacy, mystery, scope — and be consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Series-level POV consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain POV consistency across books in a series unless there's a clear, justified reason to change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can change POV between books (character death, plot reasons, author choice), but keeping POV consistent generally helps reader expectations across a series.
